en: Commentary on the Ritual Procedures for Offerings in the Mahāvairocana Sūtra,
Volume One (Fragment),
composed by the Monk Shi Bukoshi of Ryōmyō-ji Temple.
I prostrate to Vairocana Buddha, To the Dharma of True Reality, the Wisdom of Dharma, and the Law of Dependent Origination,
And to the Holy Master of Wondrous Sound (Mañjuśrīmitra), Who bestows grace so that the ocean of the nature of phenomena may be realized.

Chapter One: The Stage of Training in Mantra Practice for the Sequential Method of Offering (*Upāyapada-vidhi-mantra-caryā-vinaya-paṭala*). Regarding the explanation of the dharma of this sutra, it is analyzed through four sections: first, the statement of the general meaning; second, the explanation of its provenance; third, the interpretation of the title; and fourth, the word-by-word commentary. *The Mahāvairocana-abhisambodhi-vikurvaṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*, Chapter One: The Stage of Training in Mantra Practice for the Sequential Method of Offering. **Section One: Statement of the General Meaning** [The text proceeds with the detailed exposition of the general intent of the scripture. **Section Two: Explanation of the Provenance** [The text proceeds with the account of how the teaching was transmitted. **Section Three: Interpretation of the Title** [The text proceeds with the etymological and contextual analysis of the title. **Section Four: Word-by-Word Commentary** [The text proceeds with the detailed exegesis of the sūtra’s content. (Note: The provided source text contains only the structural outline for the first chapter. The full translation would require the subsequent prose of the commentary.)

First, regarding the statement of the general meaning: Now, the ultimate principle of true nature transcends words and is free from form; yet its manifestation in response to capacities is not a display of characteristics. This refers to the wondrous clarity of the principle through gateways such as the letter "A."

This present sutra contains profound principles within its words, yet its ultimate meaning transcends the literal text. Therefore, through the empowered spiritual power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata, it is sealed with secret mudrās and guided by mantras. For this reason, one must receive instruction from a master before entering its gate; those who are not worthy are forbidden from transmitting it recklessly, and those who have not undergone consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are prohibited from hearing it at will.
If one is able to see, hear, or pay homage to it, the sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will be extinguished;
for those who practice according to its teachings, an ocean of merit will gather within their very person.
Next, regarding the account of its origins: formerly, in Central India, there was a king who had four sons. When that king was approaching the end of his life, the queen asked him:
“Great King, after Your Majesty has passed away, which son shall succeed to the throne?
The King replied immediately,
“The youngest son shall be able to succeed to the throne.”

Thereupon, after the father-king had passed away, the ministers and all the officials assembled and inquired about his final instructions; the queen then replied exactly as the king had spoken at the time of his death.
At that time, the queen, his elder brothers, and the ministers entreated the younger son to succeed to the royal throne, but the younger son replied:
"I have made a vow to leave the household life and study the Way, hoping to deliver all living beings."
"I am not fit to succeed to the throne.
Although the Queen Mother and others entreated him with repeated urgency in accordance with his father’s final testament, the young prince declined as he had before.
After the Queen Mother and others had pleaded three times, they eventually compelled him to ascend the throne; the young prince, not daring to disobey, thereupon took the royal seat.
Thereafter, he further reflected:
"While I dwell in this country, I cannot leave the household life.
My paternal aunt is the queen of a neighboring kingdom; it would be appropriate for me to seek refuge with her, for she will surely enable me to renounce the world."
Using skillful means, he escaped and hurried toward that country.
Upon reaching its border, a local commander questioned him, saying, "Who are you?"
The youth immediately replied,
"I am the king of the kingdom of Central India.
The local commander said:
"If you are the ruler of this country, why have you come alone?

He replied, "I originally hoped to leave the household life to study the Way; had I remained long in my native land, I certainly would not have been able to leave the household life. I deeply yearned to leave the household life to study the Way."
Having prostrated, he dispatched a messenger to report this to the king.
Upon hearing of it, the queen sent someone to come and welcome him.
When the young boy saw the queen, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and declared his aspiration.
Upon hearing these words, the queen wept with sorrow, her heart filled with grief and compassion; after a long while, she said:
"Your clan is that of the Kṣatriyas; you are a descendant of Prince Śuddhodana and a distant nephew of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni."
"I have heard that Śākyamuni renounced the rank of crown prince, left the city to enter the path, and thereby attained perfect enlightenment.

Among all things in the world, the most difficult to relinquish is one's precious throne; you, like Śākyamuni, have renounced the position of a king and made a great vow—surely you shall attain Buddhahood."
From this day forward, I shall follow the ways of the common people, carrying my almsbowl to beg for food and maintaining my fast with coarse rice.
This is truly a matter for sorrow.
Nevertheless, as for the sincere vows and aspirations of a great man, there is nothing that can be done to alter them.
He then granted permission for him to leave the household life.
He invited a Dharma Master of high virtue from within the borders to serve as his preceptor, so that he might leave home and study.

The young boy possessed the nature of brilliant wisdom; upon hearing something once, he immediately grasped its profound essence, and after asking twice, he could compare it to a thousand or ten thousand points. Although he had not studied for many years, everything he learned he mastered completely.
Thereupon, the Dharma Master took his leave, saying:
"My understanding is exhausted; there is nothing further for me to expound.
I have heard that in that country dwell men of great virtue, sages and saints; it is fitting that I go to that place to study."
The young man, having received these instructions, paid his respects and withdrew.
He went to the abode of the wise teacher and pursued his studies as before.
Eventually, after traveling through more than fifty kingdoms and reaching Northern India, there was a city named Gandhāra.

The king of that country relied upon the Venerable Master to receive the dharma-recitation; however, as the text of the scripture was extensive and its meaning profound, he was unable to follow it immediately in his offerings. He therefore requested the Venerable Master for instructions on the method of making offerings.

The Upādhyāya accepted the invitation and sought the sacred empowerment at the stupa built by King Suvarṇa-śālī; suddenly, this method of offering appeared in the air, its golden characters brilliantly radiant.
The Master read it through once briefly; having clearly committed it to memory, he looked up at the sky and asked, "By whom was this created? He replied:
"I am the one who created it. He asked, "Who is 'I'?"
He said, "I am Mañjuśrī. He then summoned a scribe and had him transcribe it;
he gave one copy to the king and kept one for himself to carry with him, intending to circulate it throughout the four quarters.
The one referred to as "the junior" is the Venerable Tripitaka Master Śīlabhadra; he is this humble monk.
By an inconceivable stroke of fortune, I was able to consult the Master in person and have recorded, according to my capacity, the essential points of the Dharma I heard from him.

Third, regarding the explanation of the title: *The First Chapter on the Precepts for the Practice of Mantras in the Ritual Sequence of Offerings from the Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*. As for "Great" (*mahā*), it signifies the sense of being boundless.
Vairocana is the sun, which refers specifically to the sun of wisdom.
"Attaining Buddhahood" signifies the realization of perfect enlightenment and correct gnosis.
"Divine transformations and empowerment" refers to that which is sustained by spiritual power.
"Sūtra" (jīng) means to thread together and stitch; it is that which can explain [the meaning] herein.
"Making offerings" (gòngyǎng) refers to offerings of both principle and phenomena.
Regarding "principle" (lǐ): to realize the principle and enter into realization is what is called an offering of principle.
"Affairs" refers to exerting one's whole heart and all one's strength to prepare incense, flowers, and other offerings for the ocean-like assembly of Buddhas; this is called "affair-offering.
"Sequence" refers to the prior and posterior order of performing prostrations and the subsequent dismissal.
"Dharma" means the sense of a guiding rule or standard.
"Mantra" means that which simplifies and eliminates falsehood.
"Practice and study" means practicing and studying mantras.
As for the "abodes," there are these four kinds:
first, the self-nature of the Dharma-realm; second, the source of the teaching; third, the lineage masters; and fourth, the peaks and ridges of the Wondrous Mountain.
"Chapter" (*pinda*) refers to a category or class.
"First" means that among the five chapters of this dharma, this is the initial one; hence it is called the first.
Therefore, it is titled: *The First Chapter on the Precepts for the Practice of Mantra and the Sequential Method of Offerings from the Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisambodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*.
Fourth, regarding the word-by-word explanation, this consists of three parts: the introduction, the main exposition, and the dissemination.
The first chapter is the introduction; the next three chapters constitute the main exposition; and the final chapter is the dissemination.
Within the introductory section (*nidāna*), there are initially two verses:
the first is the "Introductory Section on Reverence and Exhortation to Believe"; from "Now, at the outset" (*atha khalu*) onwards is the "Introductory Section on Diligent Practice."
The beginning and middle consist of four sections:
the first two lines constitute the section on revering the master and extolling his virtues;
the next two lines constitute the section on that which is manifested according to the sūtras.
The next two phrases constitute the gateway of the Dharma being accomplished and bringing benefit;
the following two phrases constitute the gateway of conforming to the source and concluding the exposition.
Vairocana is here translated as "Sun."
"One who opens the pure eyes" refers to one who awakens to the subtle principle. "I" refers to Mañjuśrī.
"Making offerings" refers to offerings of both principle and phenomena.
That which is relied upon consists of the various deities.
The various ritual manuals consist of the mudrās, mantras, and so forth.
That which constitutes the sequence of accomplishment consists of prostrations and the dismissal [of the deities].
"Like that" refers to the Honored One, the Sun of Wisdom.
"Causing the original mind" means causing one to awaken to the mind whose nature is fundamentally unborn.
"My single phrase now" concludes the meaning of all that has preceded it.
The preface to the *Vīryaprayoga-sūtra* is divided into six sections:
the first full verse constitutes the Section on Accomplishing Faith and Understanding;
the second half-verse constitutes the Section on Encouraging Faith in the Triple Gem.
3. The twenty-five verses beginning with "Sentient beings' faith and understanding" constitute the section on the gate of practicing the prohibitive precepts;
4. The single verse beginning with "Abiding correctly by means of this" constitutes the section on the gate of the grave prohibitions based on the correct precepts;
5. The single verse beginning with "The gate of the sublime mantra" constitutes the section on the gate of gaining benefit through awakening the mind.
Sixth: The ten verses beginning with "Desiring" constitute the section on the attainment of Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
Within this first segment, the phrase "the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others" refers to the fruit that has been realized.
The "expedient means of the vow for unsurpassed wisdom" clarifies the ability to accomplish wisdom.
"Accomplishing that" refers to the fruit realized.
"Initiating [the mind]," and so forth, cite the fruit to reveal the cause.
Regarding the second section, the two phrases "in the fulfillment of siddhis" and "various supreme vows" collectively represent the two jewels of the Buddha and the Saṅgha;
the subsequent verses provide their individual explanations.
The "form of the mantra" refers to the body adorned with the syllables of the mantra.
"Abiding in various mudrās and dignified postures" refers to the vidyā-mudrā and lying on one's right side.
The path to be traversed is precisely the self-nature of the dharma-realm.
The Vaipulya Vehicle is the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*.
The above clarifies the definitive faith in the Three Jewels.
Question:
Regarding the homage paid to the Three Jewels here and the homage paid to the Buddha Jewel at the beginning, what is the difference in their meaning? Answer:
The first section reveals Mañjuśrī’s own expression of reverence; herein, the rules for practitioners of future generations are clarified.
Question:
Does Mañjuśrī pay homage to the Triple Gem?
Answer: It is through taking refuge and paying homage.
That which is called "I rely upon the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*" is precisely the act of revering the Dharma.
Not disparaging oneself is precisely what constitutes honoring the Sangha;
the Three Jewels as being of one essence can be understood accordingly.
Regarding the third section, those sentient beings with superior, middling, and inferior degrees of faith and understanding are precisely the beings of the six realms of existence.
Regarding the phrase "if toward the most excellent," this refers to the aforementioned *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*.
A practitioner who has been disciplined does not violate the samaya.
As for the "distinctive discipline," this refers to the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*.
"Being endowed with the conditions and constituent parts" refers to the constituent parts for constructing the *maṇḍala*.
"Abiding with a single mind" means focusing the single mind upon the master.
"Samaya" clarifies the equality of the original vows and so forth.
The "site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) refers to the wondrous and perfect altar.
The "fundamental teaching" is the *Vairocanābhisambodhi Sūtra*.
"In the presence of the Honored One" refers to the master who bestows the empowerment (abhiṣeka).
The Victorious Samaya and the Protectors are attained by those who have received the empowerment of the transmitted Dharma.
Those who practice the equality of the mantra that gathers all things rightly rest their minds unmoving within the state of original non-arising.
Regarding "entering this supreme vehicle of mantras": "entering" means understanding; the "supreme vehicle" is the very essence of the principle realized by Vairocana.
"Secret practitioner" refers to one who practices the *mantra-yāna*.
"Preceptor" (*ācārya*) refers to such masters and others.
"Vast and manifold merits" means that the preceptor is an ocean of merit, and this ocean of merit dwells within his person.
Why is this? A sutra states:

"If one wishes to see the Buddha and pay him homage, or if one wishes to make offerings to the Buddha, paying homage to and making offerings to this person is no different from doing so to the Buddha himself."
"Why is there no difference?
It is because the body is adorned with the five kinds of mantra-hearts, mudrās, and so forth.
The "Sūtra" refers to the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-sūtra*.
Regarding "nothing surpasses anger," this is as explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
"Purifying the bodhicitta" refers precisely to the mantra.

To "constantly maintain patience and not observe faults" means that among the various forms of patience regarding worldly phenomena, the most difficult to endure is toward those who betray one's kindness and virtue; therefore, one is exhorted to practice patience.
"Waiting" (俟) means to await.
What is meant by "waiting for the opportune time" refers precisely to the time when one intends to cultivate the samādhi of the mantra.
If a donor suddenly requests that you preach the Dharma, you should immediately say:
"I shall cultivate samādhi and later preach it for you.
At that time, this was not possible.

As for the pure, clear, and refined Dharma, within its essential principle there are always present the qualities of countless asaṃkhyeya *anāsrava* (outflow-free) merits and the various gates of the *pāramitās*, such as giving (*dāna*).
Regarding "by means of various liquors": these liquors are the root of heedlessness; if one drinks them, they will disturb one's samādhi.
Regarding "increasing conceit": this increases false attachment; when false attachment is deep, the practice of meditative concentration becomes even more remote.
"Those who are now equal" praises the profound meaning of these concise words.
"Causing them to understand extensively and give rise to certainty" extols the benefit of much learning.
From the beginning up to this point, the brief exposition on the principles of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom is complete.
In the fourth section, one relies on this to abide in the precept of equanimity.
As for abiding in the precept of equanimity, it means dwelling in the mind of the nature of the precepts, without giving rise to a mind that clings to the observance of precepts.
The preceding section used illustrious virtues to prohibit the causes of transgression.
Within the fifth section, regarding those who are "in accord with the awakened mind through the wondrous gateway of mantra," there are two parts:
first, the visualization of the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity); and...
When the visualization of the deity is matured, one's own body becomes the deity.
This mind not being distracted is what is meant by "correspondence through speech.
"The wise" refers to those who have realized the principle of original non-arising.
In the sixth section, "that which clarifies the Dharma" refers to the mantra.
The two lines beginning with "The wise receive from their teacher" conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.
The three and a half verses beginning with "The wondrous mountain and its auxiliary peaks" symbolize the place upon which the practitioner relies.
Within this area, there are four locations, each with its own established regulations:
First, Mount Miaoshan (Mount Wondrous), a lofty and sublime mountain.
Second, the Auxiliary Peaks (Fufeng), peaks within the embrace of the great mountain, suitable for peaceful habitation.
"Halfway up the cliff" refers to a cave within a stone wall that is habitable.
There are three kinds of *kaṅkha* (niches):
first, chamber-niches; second, earthen niches; and third, stone niches. These are called *kaṅkha* because they resemble caves and are places where honored images are installed.
"Cave" refers to a stone chamber.
"Between two mountains" refers to places where springs and rocks are pure and clean, such as locations suitable for the stability of practice or along rivers.
"Ji" refers to water chestnuts (the seeds of the *Trapa natans*).
"Hè" refers to lotus leaves.
"Jing River" refers to a river where the flowing water is constant and never ceases.
"Island" refers to a place within the water that can serve as a dwelling.
"Bank" (*tīra*) means the side or margin.
It refers to a clean place on the slope of a riverbank where one may dwell to practice the Way.
Next, the first phrase manifests the avoidance of places that are either suitable or unsuitable.
"Agitated mind" (*kūn-hsin*) means confusion and lack of stillness; it refers to being vexed and disturbed by people and things.
Third, regarding the location of grasses, trees, and forests:
"luxuriantly spreading" (*fu-shu*) describes the appearance of trees with thick, flourishing foliage.
The forests and thickets are secluded and desolate, making them suitable places for dwelling and spiritual practice.
"Milk-wood" refers to mulberry and grain trees.
"Auspicious grass" refers to the yellow *máo* grass found in this land.
The following two lines clarify what may or may not be done.
Fourth, the clarification of the locations for monasteries and stupas.
There are three types of *araṇya* (hermitages):
First is Dharma, second is Tāṇḍaka, and third is Maṇḍaka.
Dharma is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa). Tāṇḍaka is the "stainless grass."
"Maṇḍagā" refers to a place free from clamor and agitation.
What is explained herein is based on the case of Maṇḍagā.
The subsequent phrase clarifies what is permissible and what is not.
“Duty” (*vṛtti*) means activity.
The “five desires” (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) are form, sound, odor, taste, and touch.
The “envelopments and fetters” (*paryavasthāna*) are the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): stinginess and greed, ill-will, lethargy and drowsiness, restlessness and agitation, and doubt.
*Siddhi* means accomplishment, and it is also called the attainment of *bodhi*.
As for "pure livelihood," it refers to the practice of having few desires and being content.
In the language of the Hu (Indic), there are sixteen items of the *dhūta* [ascetic practices], but because they are either implicit or explicit in the sūtras and śāstras, twelve are taught here.
Sixteen: four regarding robes, six regarding food, and six regarding dwellings.
The four regarding robes are:
wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), wearing woolen robes (*vārkṣa*), wearing patched robes (*nāmatika*), and maintaining the three robes (*tricīvara*).
Regarding "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla): it refers to garments scorched by fire, gnawed by oxen, chewed by rats, or the clothes of the deceased, and so forth.
In foreign lands, such items are discarded in streets and fields; because they are like refuse, they are called "refuse-rags."
The practitioner takes [the cloth], washes, dyes, and sews it to treat it for use as clothing for his body.
Question:
Why does he accept only this kind of robe?
There are three grades:
the inferior grade consists of obtaining clothing through various wrong livelihoods, such as farming, domestic service, or trade;
the middling grade consists of avoiding the aforementioned faults and receiving robes from the Saṃgha or robes offered by lay donors.
"Upāli, he did not accept the robe from the Saṃgha, but rather accepted it from a *caitya-vyavasthita* (one who has passed away).
Why did he not accept it from the Saṃgha?

According to the Dharma of the Saṃgha, when a legal matter is to be adjudicated or administrative duties are to be assigned, one must appoint an official to preside over the proceedings; [if one acts otherwise], it disturbs the mind and causes the abandonment of the Path."
Why not refrain from them?
If one accepts them and transgresses, one will pursue robes and frequently fall into wrong livelihood.
Furthermore, it gives rise to deep attachment, making liberation difficult to attain.
Furthermore, when one receives preferential treatment from close relatives, those who do not receive it become estranged, which hinders equal transformation.
Moreover, frequent reception leads to the arising of pride, while non-reception leads to complaints.
[The donor] may be ignorant and fail to recognize the field of merit, resulting in either giving or not giving; or, feeling self-contempt and shame, they give rise to sorrow and regret.
Furthermore, he frequently visits abandoned roads and does not leave, causing resentment.
Moreover, he harbors hatred and jealousy toward good people, slandering the virtuous.
He has no desire to go there.
Seeing these many faults, one does not accept [other offerings] and even bypasses the gift of robes.
Why accept only the refuse-rag?
Because having few concerns increases the Path, and being free from faults is without transgression; therefore, one accepts only this.
Regarding "woolen robes" (*vārkṣa-cīvara*): these are made from the fine wool of birds and beasts, washed while wet.
When a practitioner has no excrement available [to use as dye], they may obtain this to serve as clothing.
Regarding "patchwork robes" (*pāṃsukūla*): these are made from decaying, old, and tattered rags, sewn together for the sake of the body, rather than wearing fine garments.
Why is this? If one seeks fine clothing, it gives rise to affliction and leads to transgression; it wastes effort and causes the abandonment of the Path.
Furthermore, while not yet having obtained fine clothing, the practitioner of the Path develops a state of greedy attachment.
Furthermore, in the wilderness, there are many dangers from bandits that may even lead to loss of life.
Regarding the "three robes," these are the five-strip robe, the seven-strip robe, and the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
Those who follow the path of superior practice accept only these three and do not keep any other garments.
Why is this? Laypeople seek pleasure and thus keep various kinds of clothing;
non-Buddhist practitioners engage in asceticism and go naked without shame.
The Buddha abides in the Middle Way, having abandoned the two extremes; therefore, he maintains three robes.
Furthermore, seeking many robes would waste effort and cause one to neglect the Path, while too few would fail to provide for one's needs; thus, he maintains three robes.
However, the three robes are sufficient for the needs of the body.
When engaged in manual labor, or when coming and going for the sake of minor or major necessities, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
For performing virtuous deeds, one wears the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*).
To transform and gather worldly people, leading them to reverence and faith, one must wear the *saṃghāṭī*.

Furthermore, one wears the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) in private places, the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṣāya*) when entering the assembly, and the *saṃghāṭī* when entering royal palaces or inhabited villages.

Furthermore, when the weather was temperate and warm, he wore the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṇṭhaka*); when it was cold, he added the seven-strip robe (*saptakaṇṭhaka*); and when the suffering of the cold became severe, he added the great outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*).

Thus, once during the height of winter, when the night air was so piercingly cold that it seemed to split one apart, the Tathāgata wore the five-strip robe during the first watch of the night; as the night grew long and the cold intensified, he added the seven-strip robe; and during the final watch of the night, when the biting cold reached its peak, he added the great outer robe.
The Buddha then thought:
"In future ages, there will be virtuous men who cannot endure the suffering of cold; for them, these three robes will be sufficient to sustain their bodies.
For these many reasons, he permitted the keeping of the three robes.

The six [rules] regarding food are: first, eating by alms; second, begging for alms in regular order; third, not consuming food that has undergone the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) procedure; fourth, eating in a single sitting; fifth, eating in a single mouthful, also called "moderation in portion"; and sixth, not drinking water after midday.
Regarding those who beg for alms, there are three types among human beings:
inferior, middling, and superior.
Those of the inferior class, though they have freely entered the homeless life, sustain themselves through wrong livelihoods.

Plowing fields and planting crops, engaging extensively in various means of livelihood, and practicing all manner of crafts—these are the various forms of wrong livelihood through which one lives at will.
As for the middling grade: having abandoned the aforementioned faults, one accepts food from the Saṃgha and also accepts invitations beyond the limit.
Those who practice the higher path do not accept food from the Sangha nor food offered by special invitation, but practice only alms-gathering.
Why do they not accept food from the Sangha or special invitations?
The fault is the same as before.
For what purpose does one practice alms-gathering exclusively? There are two reasons:
first, for one's own sake, to cultivate the path with few concerns; second, for the sake of others, to bring benefit and welfare to the world.
Regarding "one who begs for food in successive order," this is also subsumed under the general category of begging for food.

This term highlights that at the time of begging, one avoids partiality and excess; whereas, specifically speaking, ordinary fools crave flavors and abandon the poor to follow the wealthy, while those of limited practice and narrow compassion abandon the wealthy to follow the poor.

Those of the superior practice depart from greed and narrow-mindedness, extending compassion equally to all sentient beings without discriminating between the poor and the wealthy, such as by practicing sequential alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*).
Regarding the phrase "not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) rite," the Vinaya states:
although a person may practice sequential alms-gathering, they may repeatedly obtain proper food at various places of seeking and thus repeatedly eat according to the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite.
The practitioner reflects:

"Regarding this practice of leftover food (pāriśuddhi), although the World-Honored One permitted it for those who are ill, I am currently not ill and should not accept it; therefore, I shall not perform the rite of leftover food."
Since this is subsumed under the practice of eating in a single sitting (*ekāsanika*), it is generally not mentioned separately in the sūtras and śāstras.
As for the specific distinction made in the Vinaya: one who eats in a single sitting does not consume any further minor snacks after the midday meal.
This refers to the distinction made regarding the practice of abstaining from frequent eating; because these differences are observed, they are explained separately.

As for "eating in a single sitting," there are those who, although they do not eat frequently throughout the day, nevertheless consume other items such as cakes, fruits, or congey multiple times before midday.
The practitioner reflects:
"Fools nourish their bodies for the sake of increasing afflictions.
I now do so for the sake of the Path, not for the sake of nourishing the body; I do so to destroy afflictions, not to increase fetters. Therefore, I accept but one meal."
He further reflected:
"Seeking even a single meal has already hindered the Path; how much more so would seeking many meals?
Therefore, he took only one meal.
Furthermore, he contemplates that if food is taken in excess, it gives rise to greater affliction; therefore, he accepts only one meal.
Moreover, he contemplates that when food is given through the confidence of others, even a single meal is difficult to digest, let alone a large amount.
Therefore, one accepts only a single meal.
Regarding "a single morsel of food," it is also called "moderation in eating" in the sūtras;
because one stops after accepting just one [portion], it is termed "a single morsel of food."
To be frugal and eat little is called "measured eating" (mātrajñatā); how much more so for one who observes the precept of eating only once a day?

There are those who, although they have received the practice of eating only once a day, indulge themselves in eating until full during that single meal; their bellies become distended with gas, and they fall asleep to rest, remaining in this state for half the day without ceasing, which obstructs the practice of the Path. Therefore, one must exercise moderation.
Furthermore, eating too much increases afflictions (*kleśa*), making them difficult to subdue; therefore, one must moderate one's intake.
Moreover, eating too much increases drowsiness, is difficult to digest like a disease, and causes the body to be ill at ease; therefore, one must moderate one's intake.
Furthermore, because the practitioner seeks the Dharma-body and gradually abandons the food-body, they should practice moderation in their intake.
To what extent should this moderation reach?
It should be according to what one can personally endure: set aside one-third for birds and beasts to give to them, and eat the remainder oneself; even a small amount is beneficial and virtuous.

Regarding the statement "not drinking after midday," there are those who, although they regulate their food and drink, still crave flavors and consume various beverages after midday, such as fruit juices, honey syrup, and rock-sugar syrup.
In seeking this beverage, one often resorts to wrong livelihoods, wasting effort and neglecting the Path;

therefore, one does not drink it. Furthermore, observe that this mind is difficult to restrain; like a horse without a bridle that eats grass to the left and right, it cannot swiftly follow the will of the driver. Only by adding the reins and bit can it advance quickly and go according to the person's intent; thus, one must exercise restraint and sever [unwholesome tendencies].
The six abodes in the middle are:

first, dwelling in an araṇya; second, dwelling among tombs; third, dwelling at the foot of a tree; fourth, dwelling in the open air; fifth, constantly sitting; and sixth, sitting wherever one happens to be.
*Āraṇya* is translated here as "empty and secluded place.

As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, one *dhanus* consists of four *hasta*; five hundred *dhanus* from a village is called one *krośa*, and half of that is termed an *āraṇya* location, which calculates to approximately three *li*.
The practitioner of dhūta practices is extremely close to this; one should be able to distance oneself from it for the sake of greater benefit. Why is this so?
Because the practitioner forms this thought:
"When I was formerly at home, I was bound by my parents and relatives; for this reason, I renounced them.

Now that I have left the household life, if I were again to become attached to my teachers, disciples, fellow students, and spiritual friends, it would be no different from being in the secular world."
Therefore, one must abandon [residence in] villages and dwell in an araṇya.
Furthermore, because villages are crowded with men and women, they greatly increase worldly defilements; it is not appropriate to live therein.
Moreover, being near a village, the clamor of sounds and noise hinders the cultivation of the concentrated mind.

Regarding "dwelling among tombs" (*śmāśānika*): among tombs there are many corpses that are putrid, bloated, and foul-smelling; by beholding this filth, it is easy to enter the gateway of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Furthermore, the corpses in tombs are decomposed, having been broken down by being consumed by fire or scattered and extinguished; by beholding them, it is easy to enter the gateway of the meditation on impermanence (*anityatā-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, in a charnel ground, bones are scattered and disarrayed; seeing them makes it easy to enter the contemplation of emptiness and non-self.
Therefore, he stays in a charnel ground.

As for "under a tree," because he had previously stayed in a charnel ground, observed a corpse, and accomplished the task of attaining the Way, he left the charnel ground and came to stay under a tree.

Furthermore, although he previously took the sign of a corpse in a cemetery, there were many sounds such as wailing and lamentation that obstructed his practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā; therefore, he came beneath a tree to bind his mindfulness and engage in contemplative investigation.
Furthermore, the shade of the trees provides shelter equivalent to half a house; thus he stays beneath the trees to dwell in peace and cultivate the Way.
Moreover, since most Buddhas, sages, and those who have attained the Way or realized the fruits of enlightenment rely upon trees, he stays beneath the trees.
Regarding those who sit in the open air: dwelling for long periods under the shade and dampness of trees leads to affliction; therefore, one goes to the open air.
Furthermore, there are many birds and small fowl upon the trees, whose clamorous sounds disturb the cultivation of meditative concentration; therefore, one remains in the open air.

Furthermore, because the practitioner has stayed long beneath trees, an attachment to the trees arises in the mind; or else, one discriminates between this tree as good and that as bad. To eliminate these afflictions, it is necessary to abandon the trees and come to an open space.
Because it is clearly and manifestly revealed as being unobstructed, he stays in the open air.
Furthermore, because the moonlight illuminating the open air makes the mind and thoughts clear and pure, facilitating entry into meditative concentration, he stays in the open air.

Regarding the practitioner who always sits: among the four modes of deportment, walking and standing are too arduous, while lying down is too indulgent; sitting avoids these two extremes and is capable of being maintained for a long duration, therefore one must always sit.
Furthermore, when walking or standing, the mind becomes restless and is difficult to restrain;
when lying down, one falls into dullness and enters sleep;
whereas sitting avoids both dullness and restlessness; therefore, one must always sit.

Furthermore, for one seeking the Way whose great task remains unfinished, the thieves of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) constantly watch for an opportunity; thus, it is inappropriate to sleep peacefully, and one must therefore practice constant sitting (*prahāṇa*).
Moreover, much can be accomplished while in this middle state; food is easily digested and the breath is harmonized, and for these reasons, one must always sit.

Regarding the term "sitting according to circumstances" (*yathāsaṃstarika*): it means sitting wherever a grass mat is available as one finds it; hence it is called "sitting according to circumstances.
When subdivided individually, there are sixteen such types.
However, the sūtras and śāstras, based on this, combine those that are implicit and explicit to proclaim twelve.
According to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, there are two categories regarding robes, four regarding food, and six regarding dwellings, totaling twelve. Regarding the two types of robes:
first, wearing the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe); second, wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*). All others are not discussed here.
Regarding the four types of food: first, alms-food; second, food not prepared by the *kṛtānna* method; third, eating in a single sitting; and fourth, eating in a single mouthful.
"Begging in sequence" is included within the category of alms-food.
Regarding the statement that one should not drink even thin gruel after midday, this is subsumed within the rule for "one sitting" (ekāsana) and therefore is not discussed separately.
The six rules concerning location are the same as above.
According to the *Dvādaśa-sūtra*, there are three rules established for clothing, three for food, and six for location, totaling twelve.

Regarding the three matters concerning clothing: first, wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*); second, wearing garments of wool; third, maintaining the three robes (*tricīvara*). All other matters are not discussed here. Regarding the three matters concerning food:
namely, begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*), eating in a single sitting (*ekāsana*), and eating a single morsel (*ekagrāsa*).
All other [prohibitions] are not mentioned here, as they are subsumed within the practice of sequential alms-gathering (*piṇḍapāta*).

Eating food for which the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of declaring one has had enough) has not been performed, and not drinking non-liquid refreshments after midday, are subsumed within the practice of eating in a single sitting (*ekāsana*).
The six dwellings are as described above.
In the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are further differences from the preceding account.
Regarding the two types of robes: wearing the *nāṃgaka* (patchwork robe) and wearing the three robes (*tricīvara*) are the same as in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

There are five [practices] regarding food: first, eating by alms; second, begging for food in systematic order; third, eating in a single sitting; fourth, moderation in food; and fifth, not drinking liquids after midday.
The practice of *khalupaścādbhaktika* (not taking further food) is subsumed within *ekāsanika* (eating at one sitting) and is not established as a separate category.
Five [practices] are explained as being intermediate; with the exception of *yathāsaṃstarika* (using whatever seat is available), the rest are as described above.
One who practices according to what has been explained above is called a person of pure livelihood (*pariśuddhājīva*).

Even if one acts in accordance with what has been taught above, if they still seek fame and profit, they are called an impure practitioner, a person of wrong livelihood, and a great thief within the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, the Sūtra says, "When various ghosts see this, they sweep away their footprints"; this is precisely its meaning.
The explanation of pure livelihood is concluded.
Below, the impure practices of wrong livelihood are explained.
There are four types of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*):
first, eating from one direction; second, eating by looking upward; third, eating from what is left behind; and fourth, eating from below.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 2, states: "The five dharmas of wrong livelihood are:..."

"First, feigning eccentricity; second, befriending oneself; third, inciting agitation; fourth, alternation between suppression and exaltation; fifth, seeking profit through profit. Regarding 'feigning eccentricity':

there are those who, out of greed for gain and offerings, may practice such ascetic dhūta disciplines as dwelling in the forest (āraṇyaka), wearing rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika), constantly begging for food (piṇḍapātika), eating at a single sitting (aikāsanika), remaining in a seated posture (naiṣadyika), or not drinking liquids after midday."
They form this thought:
"By performing such practices, one obtains offerings and respect; perhaps I too shall obtain them by performing such practices.
For the sake of gain and honor, they alter their deportment; this is called "pretending to be extraordinary."
2. Regarding "acting as one's own relative": there are those who, craving gain and offerings, go to the house of a donor and say:

"I am no different from your parents, brothers, sisters, or other relatives. If you have anything you need, I can provide it; if there is anything that must be done, I will do it for you. I do not consider distance when coming to inquire after you; my staying here is solely for your sake."
"Seeking offerings and being greedily attached to donors, using words and speech to solicit the hearts of others—such as these are called 'those who are intimate with themselves.
Third, the agitators: there are those who do not consider the sin of greed, desiring to obtain wealth and property, and putting on the appearance of one who has already acquired them."
He spoke thus: "This bowl is excellent;
or this robe is excellent; or this door-bolt is excellent; or this sitting mat (niṣīdana) is excellent. If I were to obtain these, I would be able to make use of them."
He further said,
"One who can give according to their inclination is difficult to find.
Then, going to the house of a donor, he spoke these words:
"Your family's soup, rice, cakes, and sweets are complete and delicious, and your clothing is also fine.
You constantly make offerings to me; as we have been close for a long time, I shall certainly grant you [what you desire].
To manifest such signs of greed in this manner is called "inciting."
Fourth, regarding the "willow and poplar" [type]:

there are those who, out of greed for gain and offerings, say to a donor, "You are so extremely stingy that you cannot even give to your parents, brothers, sisters, wife, children, or relatives; who then could possibly obtain anything from you?"
The donor felt ashamed and, with a mixture of reluctance and deference, made the offering.
He then went to other households and said:
"You are fortunate; you have received this human body not in vain, for an Arhat constantly enters and leaves your home, sitting and rising with you and conversing with you."
Having formed this thought, he conceives this intention toward the donor:
"No one else enters or leaves my house; they must surely think it was I.
This is called *liuyang*.
5. Seeking profit from profit: There is someone who, taking up articles for livelihood such as robes, alms bowls, outer cloaks (*saṃghāṭī*), or sitting mats (*niṣīdana*), says to another person:
"The king, or those like the king, or other noblemen have given these things to me."
He had this thought: "The donor might think:
'If even those kings and nobles can provide offerings, why should I not do so?'"
This person, by means of these gains, further seeks other gains; therefore, this is called "seeking gain through gain.

If one follows the practice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the practitioner holds their heart up to show the Buddha. With this body and mind, whether facing humans or animals, or even facing a wall as if it were a human face, they do not commit evil anywhere; because the Buddhas rejoice in this, it is said that one follows the practice of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Regarding "firm faith and understanding in the true mantra": this means that one knows this mantra flows from the pure *dharmadhātu*; by the power of this wisdom, one maintains firm faith and understanding that is as immovable and unshakable as a vajra.

One who possesses the power of pure wisdom and is able to endure understands that these deluded thoughts arise within this body and mind; when deluded thoughts cease, they are like the eight winds passing through the great void, which remain unmoved. Therefore, it is said that the power of wisdom is able to endure.

Regarding "vigorously seeking nothing of the world": one should cast aside fame and profit as if they were mucus or spittle; one must not look back with the mind, which is like a rotting corpse, but should seek *siddhi* directly as if one's head were on fire. Therefore, it is said that one practices vigor without seeking the world.

Always delighting in what is firm and steadfast, and being without cowardice or weakness, one is courageous and diligent like a vajra; following [the path] without fail like a lion, one is therefore firm and steadfast, and not cowardly or weak.

Regarding "achieving accomplishment for oneself and others in the present life": seeing others obtain benefit as if one had obtained it oneself, and if one sees oneself obtain benefit, necessarily giving it to others; therefore, it is called achieving accomplishment for oneself and others.

Regarding "not following other deities and relying on fearlessness": one dwells with the mind focused on the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and proceeds directly in practice; even if hearing praises of other deities from the side, one does not waver. Therefore, it is said that one does not follow other deities and relies on fearlessness.

One who possesses these is called a "virtuous companion," for all worldly and supramundane virtues are met with joy by both ordinary beings and noble ones alike; therefore, it is said that one possesses such a virtuous companion.
Chapter Two: Increasing and Guarding Pure Conduct (Part One). Regarding the explanation of this chapter, it shall be analyzed through four sections.

First, regarding the explanation of the names: it is called "guarding" (*rakṣā*) because one protects the precepts and preserves the person by practicing in accordance with the pure conduct of their nature; it is called "augmenting" (*vṛddhi*) because one necessarily attains the fruit through such practice.

2. Regarding the purpose of this chapter: The pure precepts were explained in the preceding chapter; this chapter is able to protect those who uphold what was taught. For this reason, this second chapter follows.
Regarding the three points of essential purpose (*piṭaka-artha*): practitioners who cultivate the path receive the power of the Dharma and take this chapter as their primary object of veneration.
By employing the indestructible body to abide in the Buddha-mind, they realize it for themselves and awaken others; this is the ultimate aim of this chapter.
Fourth, regarding the summary of the text: this chapter consists largely of two parts:
first, the initial two and a half verses, which serve as the general introduction to the chapter;
second, the section beginning with "Next, at the navel," which provides the detailed explanation.
In the initial general introduction, the first two lines conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one.

Regarding "daily first abiding in mindfulness and wisdom": "daily" means from the day one receives the Dharma and begins practice until the attainment of Buddhahood; during this interval, one does not omit [practice] during the three periods of the day, hence the term "daily."
"Mindfulness and wisdom" refers to mindfulness of the teacher and wisdom.

"Resting in accordance with the Dharma" means lying on one's right side with the right hand as a pillow and the left hand extended over the thigh, pressing down upon it; this is precisely what that means.
Regarding "the time of initial arising," it refers to the night of receiving the Dharma, specifically the latter part of that night when the sign of dawn appears.
As for "obstacles," the cycle of birth and death has the three poisons of affliction as its root;
to realize that these three poisons of affliction are fundamentally unarisen is itself the removal of obstacles.
"This night" refers to the long night of birth and death prior to receiving the Dharma.
"Sins produced by negligence" refers to the sins produced by the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects.
"Zealous" means reciting according to the Dharma with the urgency of one whose head is on fire.
"Tranquil faculties" means realizing that the root does not arise.
"Possessing a mind of compassion and benefit" means using wisdom to distinguish oneself from the inferior Hīnayāna, thereby manifesting the courage and vigor of great compassion.
Regarding the vow to deliver others: as long as the realm of sentient beings is not exhausted, my aspiration shall not cease.
Regarding bathing according to the Dharma: for external bathing, one must necessarily use fragrant water.
Alternatively, regarding "not bathing," it refers to the inner bath that realizes the dharma of no-body which can be bathed.
Second, in the detailed explanation, there are fifteen mantras, which constitute fifteen gates; each gate contains both verses and mantras.

Regarding the verse, "a fasting chamber in a secluded place" refers to the maṇḍala constructed in locations such as the peaks and ridges of Mount Myōsan; it is the chamber for recitation and the attainment of *siddhi*.

Regarding "scattering exquisite flowers and the like": in all offerings, one should carefully distinguish each according to the nature and category of the respective deities and their positions within the maṇḍala, ensuring that their color, fragrance, flavor, and texture are pleasing to the human mind.
Among the three colors—white, yellow, and red—the Tathāgata family should employ white, the Lotus family yellow, and the Vajra family red.

Furthermore, one should act according to the orientations within the maṇḍala: for a circular altar, use white; for a square altar, use yellow; for a triangular altar, use red; and for the various worldly deities, use red.
The *padma* is the red lotus; blue, yellow, white, and other varieties of water-born lotuses may all be offered to the various Honored Ones.
As for the dragon-tree flower (*nāgapuṣpa*), it was beneath this tree that the World-Honored One Maitreya attained Buddhahood.
As for what is called the *nāgakesara* flower, it is a flower esteemed among dragons and its species is quite common in the West.
The *ketaka* flower and the *sāla* tree flower are both native to India and do not exist in this region.
Whatever things the human heart delights in and which the world regards as auspicious, all may be offered.

One should carefully examine each one with mindfulness, gathering them to form a garland for variegated adornment—whether by stitching or knotting—so that, because of the practitioner’s earnest, pure, and profound mind, the Honored Ones will be pleased and grant their protective regard.
"Placing accordingly" refers to the hall previously constructed.
"The Canon" refers to the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*.
Regarding the instruction to "rely upon the direction where the principal deity resides," one interpretation states:
It is the direction in which the principal deity (honzon) resides within the recitation hall (nenjūdō).

A second interpretation states that the directions are manifested according to the capacities of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions; thus, it is appropriate for [the deity] to be in the east as Yakushi, in the west as Amitābha, or on Mount Qingliang as Mañjuśrī, and so forth.
"Abiding with single-mindedness" means binding the mind to the *iṣṭadevatā* (honored deity) without momentarily averting the eyes, and so forth.
"The five wheels" refers to the five limbs of the body.

"Taking refuge" (*namas*) means that among all things cherished by sentient beings, life is the most precious; using this treasure-store as an offering to the Triple Gem through mantras, mudrās, and the like.
Regarding "purifying the actions of body, speech, and mind": it refers to the pure action of speech when, at the moment of death, one takes refuge in the Honored One.
Regarding "the expedient means of prostration within the mantra": it refers to the true words (mantras) by which one performs this prostration.
The mantra is itself the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇajñāna*); all honored ones take this wisdom of the true mark as their body and mind.

By reciting the mantra of the wisdom of the true mark, one immediately reaches the honored ones of the wisdom of the true mark; since these honored ones of the wisdom of the true mark simultaneously and instantaneously receive the prostration of the mantra, it is said that one is thus able to universally prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The passage beginning with "Kneeling with the right knee on the ground" describes the mantra-gate of the skillful means for expiating transgressions.
The recitation of the mantra is the same as before.

Since the wisdom of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇajñāna*) is itself free from transgression, if one clings to the notion that there is transgression, this very wisdom can cause one to realize the absence of transgression; therefore, it is called "expiating transgression."
"Homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time," and so forth, constitutes the third refuge: the Expedient Means of the Mantra Gate.

Beyond the wisdom of these mantras there is no delusion; that which is free from external delusion is itself the mantra. When one recites this mantra and awakens to the reality of one's own nature, it is therefore called "taking refuge."
There is also the recitation of mantras.
In the verses, "Namo" means "to deliver me," and it is also said to mean "to pay homage.
The "three kinds of eternal bodies" refer to the three bodies, such as the Dharma-body and so forth.
Realizing that birth and death are fundamentally unborn, one speaks of the "eternal body" (nitya-kāya).

As for the "Treasury of the True Dharma" (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka): "True" (saddha) means to exclude the heterodox; "Dharma" (dharma) means the guiding principle; and "Treasury" (kośa) means to contain virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The "multitude of great resolve" refers to those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

From the passage "I purify this body, free from all defilements" onwards is the fourth section, the Mantra Gate of the Expedient Means of Offering the Body; here too, there is the recitation of mantras.

Apart from the true body (*dharmakāya*), there is no other body; the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are likewise of one and the same essence. Sentient beings delusively cling to the notion that there are distinct bodies, yet this gateway of mantras enables them to realize that their own bodies and the Buddha’s body are equal and without distinction; therefore, it is called "bestowing the body."

From "The Jewel of the Supreme Vow of the Pure Bodhicitta" onwards is the fifth section, the Gate of Mantras for the Expedient Means of Arousing Bodhicitta, which includes the prose recitation of the mantras.

Since there is no distinction between my body and the Buddha’s body, and the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom is identical to my own wisdom, this mantra causes one to realize this Dharma and enables one to know how to generate the aspiration for bodhi.
"Augmentation" refers to the addition that can manifest the meaning of the mantra.
"Bodhicitta" is the self-awakening to the purity of one's own nature.
"Citta" carries the sense of the central reality; therefore, it is said to be "detached from all [extremes]," and so forth.
"Aggregates" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*).
"Elements" refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
"Bases" refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
The grasper is the deluded mind;
the grasped is the deluded object.
To "discard" means to be detached from them.
That "dharmas have no self" means being free from delusive objects and the like.
That "one's own mind is equal" means the absence of discursive thought.
Furthermore, "one's own mind" refers to the mind of discursive thought itself.
"Equanimity" means that the deluded thoughts of one's own mind are fundamentally unarisen; therefore, it is said that the grasper and the grasped, and so forth, are originally unarisen.
"Like the great void" means that within the great sun-wheel of wisdom, there is no distinction between the day and night of birth and death.
Regarding "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*): the sun of wisdom is itself the body.
By upholding the non-arising of delusion so that it accords with true nature, it is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
This is an interpolated phrase added by the translator to praise the Sanskrit original.
If one is able to recite the Sanskrit original, that is foremost; however, it is also permissible to recite by grasping the meaning according to the Chinese text.
As for the "Dharma-assembly" (dōjō), it is the field of tranquility (*śānta-pada*).

From the passage "In the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions" onwards is the sixth section, the Mantra-gate of the Expedient Means of Rejoicing (*anumodana-upāya-mantramukha*), which also includes the recitation of mantras.
The wisdom of reality itself is free from envy; this envy-free wisdom causes one to be without hatred or jealousy.
By sincerely reciting this true wisdom, one ensures that it does not deviate from the wisdom of ultimate reality; therefore, it is called the skillful method of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
"From 'I now entreat all Tathāgatas' onwards is the seventh section, the Gate of Mantras for Entreaty through Expedient Means; the verses and mantras are the same as before.
With true wisdom and great compassion, they constantly benefit sentient beings; because they benefit sentient beings, they descend with the rain of Dharma."
To recite this mantra with utmost sincerity in order to entreat the Dharma to remain in the world is called "Exhortation.

From the words "May it cause ordinary beings to dwell in their respective places" onwards is the eighth section: the Mantra Gate of Expedient Means for Entreating the Dharmakāya; the verses and the mantra are the same as before.

The Dharmakāya eternally abides in its original reality; because it eternally abides, it causes one to reach the Dharmakāya. By reciting this mantra to directly invoke [the deity], it is called the "Method for the Expedient Invocation."
"From 'All virtuous karmas thus cultivated' onwards is the ninth dedication, the gateway of the expedient mantra. The verse and the mantra are the same as before.

Since the fundamental awakened true wisdom does not scatter outwardly, it is identical to dedication by virtue of this non-scattering. Diligently and with hardship one recites this mantra; returning to the fundamental Dharma of truth is what is called dedication."
"Furthermore, performing all other meritorious deeds," and so forth, is the tenth entry into the gate of the Vidyā of the Buddha-samaya; this is the body born of the Dharma.
Within this section are verses, seals (mudrās), and mantras.
"Whatever remains" refers to that which is outside of the recitation of mantras.
"Universal purification" means causing impurities within one's own three karmas not to arise.
"Compassionate rescue and protection" means causing impurities within the three karmas of others not to arise.
The "nature of mind" refers to the fact that the fundamental nature of the mind is inherently pure.
"The body conforms to what is appropriate" means facing the deity (iṣṭadevatā).
Furthermore, among the three families or five families, it refers to identifying which deity is one's own personal deity (mūladevatā).

Regarding "sitting peacefully," the crown of the head, the nose, and the navel are all held perfectly upright; this refers to the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), and so forth.
Regarding "purifying the three paths of action," it means not giving rise to impurity through the three types of action; this itself is the path.
The seal (*mudrā*) is the body upon which the mantra relies.
Question:
How are the body and wisdom distinguished?
Answer:
The body is that upon which all merits rely, while wisdom (jñāna) has the meaning of illumination; thus, they are distinct in terms of their functions but one in terms of their essence.

The *Buddhasamayoga-vidyādhara-tantra* states: "At that time, the Bhagavān dwelt in the empowerment of the vast Dharma-realm, and at that very moment, he dwelt in the Samādhi of the Matrix of the Dharma-realm."

Regarding the phrase "Emerging from this samādhi, he spoke the Vidyādhara of the Buddha-samaya": the Sanskrit term *vipula* carries the meaning of "vast" or "extensive," referring to that which is profoundly and boundlessly expansive, beyond all measure.
The intrinsic nature of all such phenomena is called the Vimala Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all Buddhas, the true reality of mantras, and the true reality of sentient beings are all the Vimala Dharma-realm; because they mutually empower one another through this, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, just as when a man and woman unite, the causal seed is entrusted to the womb and is not lost or destroyed—this is the meaning of mutual empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

In the same way, when the Buddhas and kings, with their consorts as queens, harmoniously unite to produce the *Vibhūṣaṇa* (Viśvabharā) seed, it is sustained by the Womb of Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā-garbha*) and remains without loss or destruction; therefore, it is called the empowerment of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-adhiṣṭhāna*).

The World-Honored One universally empowered all sentient beings, having completed the act of making them all equal seeds, immediately entered the Samādhi of the Womb-Treasury Pervading the Dharma Realm. He beheld that each and every seed was Vairocana upon a lotus pedestal, with an inexhaustible adornment of universal gate retinues, no different from the Great Compassion Maṇḍala.

Yet, because sentient beings have not yet been able to realize this for themselves, they are said to be within the *garbha* (womb) of the Sage; when they emerge from this treasury, it is the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Having thus observed in this manner, the Bhagavān immediately arose from samādhi and spoke the vidyādhara-samaya.
*Samaya* means equality, it means the original vow, it means the removal of obstacles, and it means awakening.

Regarding "equality," it means that when the Tathāgata directly realizes this samādhi, he perceives that the various bodies, speech, and minds of all sentient beings are entirely equal to those of the Tathāgata; their meditative concentration and wisdom, as well as their body of the true mark (*dharmatākāya*), are ultimately equal; and they are ultimately equal from the moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment until the fulfillment of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Therefore, he utters words of solemn truth to inform all sentient beings:

"If what I have spoken is certainly not false, then when all sentient beings likewise utter these words of solemn truth, they too shall receive the empowerment of the three mysteries, and their inexhaustible adornments shall become equal to those of the Tathāgata."
For this reason, it is able to perform the vajra-activity; therefore, it is called *samaya*.

As for the "original vow," when the Tathāgata realized this *samaya* through direct manifestation, he saw that all sentient beings possess the potential to attain Buddhahood. Consequently, he immediately established this great vow:
"I shall now, by means of the universal gate and immeasurable skillful means, cause all sentient beings to reach unsurpassed bodhi."
Until the realm of sentient beings is entirely exhausted, my activities shall never cease.
If there are sentient beings who, in accordance with my original vow, utter these words of truth, I shall also cause all their undertakings to become entirely of the nature of vajra.
Therefore, it is called *samaya*.

As for "removing obstacles," the Tathāgata perceives that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatadharmadhātu*; yet, due solely to a single moment of ignorance (*avidyā*), they fail to realize it, even though it is constantly before their eyes.
Therefore, he utters these words of sincere truth:
"I shall now employ various skillful means to skillfully resolve and remove the cataracts from the eyes of all sentient beings.

If this vow of mine is destined to be fulfilled, then when all sentient beings follow my skillful means and speak these words of sincere truth, may they obtain the stainless eye throughout their entire lives, with all obscurations and hindrances completely exhausted."
Therefore, it is called *samaya*.

Regarding the meaning of "awakening": because all sentient beings are asleep in ignorance and thus do not themselves realize such merits, the Tathāgata moves them with truthful words to cause them to awaken.
Furthermore, by this means, I awaken all bodhisattvas and others, causing them to arise from the cave of profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and learn the lion’s stretch.
"If there are practitioners of mantras who proclaim this samaya, we Buddhas shall likewise remember our original vows and must not transgress them."
It is like a king who, having established his own laws, then personally reveres and complies with them by practicing them himself;
therefore, it is called *samaya*.
As for "Vidyādhara," in Sanskrit it is called *dhāraṇī*.

"Vidyā" refers to the practice of upholding all vidyā-gates; because one does not leak or lose anything from the time this samaya vow is undertaken until its conclusion, it is called "Entering the Buddha’s Samaya Vidyādhara."

The first phrase, "I take refuge in all Buddhas," is explained as above. The second phrase says "unequaled" (asama), and the next says "threefold equality" (tri-sama); when these are connected with the following phrase, they constitute the "Unequaled Threefold Equality Samaya."
Furthermore, "A" signifies that all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; this is the essential nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
"Sa" signifies truth. "Mi" signifies samādhi.
"Polishing" (ma) is the great emptiness of self-realization; it is also the meaning of "self" (ātman).

When the World-Honored One realized this samādhi, he clearly observed that within the minds of each and every sentient being, the universal mandala was equal to his own. Therefore, there is nothing further to be compared or contrasted with it, and thus it is called "unequaled."

The "threefold equality" refers to the equality of the three periods of time, the equality of the three causes, the equality of the three paths of action, and the equality of the three vehicles; this serves as a further explanation of the meaning of the preceding statement regarding why there is no inequality.
*Tara* means that the mind is in accordance with its true nature (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*), wherein all defilements have never arisen from the beginning.

The various skillful means employed by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time are entirely for the sake of this one great causal event (*ekamahā-kārya-hetu-pratyaya*); this is precisely the meaning of "removing obstructions."

The conclusion states: "Samaya" means the definitive lion’s roar that explains the meaning of the equality of all dharmas. Therefore, one establishes a great vow, intending to cause all beings to attain the same state as oneself, and desiring to universally open the Buddha's knowledge and vision for all sentient beings. For this reason, it serves as an awakening call for both sentient beings and all Buddhas.
Therefore, this samaya is called the Vajra Vow of All Tathāgatas; if one does not first recite and maintain it, one shall not perform any ritual activities of the mantras.

When the Bhagavān had spoken this samaya by means of his body, speech, and mind wheels, which pervade all buddha-fields, there was not one among the assembly of all the sons of the Buddhas who did not hear it.
Having heard this, one must not dare to transgress any of the dharmas of mantra. Why is this?
If a bodhisattva forms various views of inequality regarding sentient beings and all phenomena, they then violate the samaya dharma.
If one forms various limited or discriminatory thoughts regarding this vow of equality, one also transgresses the samaya dharma.
Furthermore, if whatever one does conforms to worldly fame and profit rather than being for the sake of the great causal conditions, one also transgresses the samaya dharma.
If one is negligent and indolent, failing to awaken the mind, one also transgresses the samaya-dharma.
Because of this transgression of the samaya-dharma, various obstacles arise; thus, one harms oneself and others, resulting in no benefit or merit.
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should uphold this samaya, guarding it as they would their own lives and not daring to transgress it.
Those who can purify the stage of the Tathāgata—by reciting mantras and forming mudrās—are able to eliminate both the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations.
The perfection of the stage (*bhūmi-pāramitā*) is fulfilled by purifying all obscurations, which is entirely the manifestation of the merits of the Buddha-stage.
To accomplish the realm of the path of the three dharmas refers to the seals (*mudrā*), mantras, and the secret of the mind (*manomaya-guhya*).
The "Dharmadhātu" (Realm of Reality) is the fruit itself; taken together, they constitute the fruit of the three dharmas.
From the section "Next, the Binding of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu" onwards is the eleventh: the Mantra Gate of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu.
This is the body that nurtures the Dharma; herein lies the seal, mantra, and verse.

Regarding the scripture’s statement, “The Bhagavat further spoke the Mantra of the Arising of the Dharmadhātu”: when the World-Honored One previously entered the Samādhi of the Matrix of the Dharmadhātu, he beheld that all sentient beings possess the seed of Bodhi and are equal to all Buddhas; therefore, he spoke of entering the Vidyādhara of the Buddha-Samaya.
By means of this vidyā-dhara, one attains entry into the equality of the Buddha’s precepts; this is precisely what it means to entrust oneself to the womb of the holy embryo (*āryagarbha*).

At that time, the World-Honored One again surveyed all with his universal eye and saw that all sentient beings were fully endowed with the holy embryo and born into the family of the Buddha; at that moment, the Inexhaustible Adornment was also equal to the Tathāgata.
Having arisen from this samādhi, he immediately spoke the mantra for the arising of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, observing with the universal eye (*samantacakṣus*), he saw that each and every sentient being was fully accomplished in the vajra-activities; at that time, the inexhaustible adornments were likewise equal to those of the Tathāgata.
Having arisen from this samādhi, he immediately spoke the mantra of Vajrasattva;
therefore, these three are all called samayas.
Furthermore, by entering the Buddha-samaya, one is not allowed to perish prematurely within the matrix (garbha).
Because he is born from the *dharmadhātu*, at the moment of his first emergence from the womb, he is free from all obstacles.
Because he is Vajrasattva, he is able to sustain his family estate and master all arts and crafts.

Furthermore, by means of the empowerment of the Secret Womb (Guhyagarbha) through entering the Buddha-samaya; by means of the empowerment of the two-fold retinue of Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattvas through the empowerment of the Dharmadhātu-world; and by means of the empowerment of Vajrasattva into various forms according to their respective types—entering the Buddha-samaya is like the lotus-womb, the arising from the Dharmadhātu is like the blooming of the lotus, and the accomplishment of Vajrasattva as the fruit of the lotus which returns once more to the seed: therefore, these three kinds are all termed samaya.
*Dharmadhātu* means the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
*Sarvabhāva* refers to self-nature (*svabhāva*), also called fundamental nature (*mūlasvabhāva*).
*Padaham* means "I" (*aham*).
The meaning of this phrase is that "I" is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
With the definitive lion’s roar, he declares:
"I and all sentient beings are all the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*."
"This is the meaning of equality.
'I shall always employ various skillful means to cause all sentient beings to fully realize and know [this]'—
this is the meaning of my original vow."
"Because one realizes that 'I' is the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*, one is able to eliminate all conceptual discrimination and open up pure knowledge and vision.
This is the meaning of "removing obstructions.
"May all Buddhas please remember and uphold their original vows, so that this body of mine may become identical to the nature of the *dharmadhātu* of Vairocana."
This is the meaning of "awakening. It shall be explained extensively by means of the *akṣara-dvāra* (gateways of syllables).
As for "the self-nature of the dharmadhātu," this reveals the essence of the dharma that is the object of contemplation; that is to say, it is the very essence of the wisdom of Mahāvairocana.
"Observing one's own body" reveals the practitioner's wisdom capable of such observation.
The two lines beginning with "Or by means of reality" indicate that this is not limited to mental action alone, but also involves reciting mantras with the mouth.
The "three turnings" refers to three cycles.
The four lines beginning with "One should see the abiding essence of the Dharma" clarify the benefits obtained by the practitioner.
The section beginning with "In order to make that firm" constitutes the twelfth Vajrasattva Mantra-gate; this is the body of the firm Dharma, and it further includes mudrās, mantras, and verses.
"To cause that [person] to be firm" means to make firm the body and mind of the practitioner who wishes to arise according to the *dharmadhātu*.
"Contemplating one's own vajra-body" means to be identical with the body of Vajrasattva.
The two lines of verse beginning with "Binding the Vajra-jñāna-mudrā" clarify the mudrās to be performed.
The two phrases beginning with "This person shall before long" demonstrate the benefits of performing these mudrās.
The two lines beginning with "Mantra and mudrā" manifest the characteristics perceived by the Savior of the World.
The two lines beginning with "Constantly revolving like a precious wheel" cite the physical precious wheel among what is perceived by the Savior of the World as a metaphor for the Dharma-wheel.
Regarding the Vajrasattva Mantra-gate: since the first phrase is about to explain the Vajrasattva mantra, one takes refuge in all vajras.
This means that from immeasurable gateways, one upholds the Tathāgata’s vajra-wisdom, causing all to remember, maintain, and protect it with mindfulness.
The next line says: *vajratama-ku-haṃ*. This means that my own body is identical to the vajra;
it is the self-nature of the dharmadhātu. Because it has accomplished great, firm, and solid power and cannot be dismembered or destroyed, it is described by an alternative designation as "vajra."
The Tathāgata observes with the universal eye that the adamantine wisdom-body (*vajrajñānakāya*) of all sentient beings is no different from his own; this is the meaning of equality.

Because sentient beings do not realize this for themselves, he performs various adamantine activities through immeasurable gates of adamantine wisdom, intending to destroy such great obstructions and lead them to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); this is the meaning of his original vow.
Thus, this reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) is called the Stainless Eye-Vajra; it carries the meaning of "removing obstructions.
By means of this lion’s roar, one causes the Buddha-fields of the ten directions to tremble; this carries the meaning of "arousing awareness."
Therefore, it is called *samaya*.
Furthermore, by means of the first *samaya*, the practitioner of mantra attains a body equal to the secret body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgata.
By means of the second samaya, one attains a body of extraordinary majesty, identical to the Tathāgata’s empowerment within the Palace of the Dharma-realm.
By means of the third samaya, this present physical body is transformed into vajra, and one is surrounded by a retinue of immeasurable Vajradharas.

The Buddha taught that the first samaya is for one's own enjoyment; the second samaya is for the sake of accomplishing the dharma-nature body for all bodhisattvas; and the third samaya is for the sake of subduing and gathering sentient beings according to their respective types.

The Buddha taught that the first samaya is for the purpose of establishing the Mahāvairocana Maṇḍala of the Matrix of Great Compassion; the second samaya is for performing the activities of the Vairocana-ācārya; and the third samaya is for performing the activities of the Vajradhara disciple.
